chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
title: Booing in Paris again with Nat Cole, and Panassie's traditionalism
summary: At the Salle Pleyel with Nat Cole the audience booed the opening French band, and Collins calls Panassie shortsighted for rejecting everything after Dixieland.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: When I returned to Paris with Nat Cole, we were doing a concert at the Salle Pleyel, and we had a French group to come on before we came on, see. So they played a few tunes and the people didn't want to hear them, they wanted to hear Nat. And so they started booing the band, so the band stopped playing and booed the audience. You know. But Pannassié, as everyone knows, he's a strict traditionalist, you know. He opposes anything other than Dixieland, I imagine. This is where he's coming from. So everything else is taboo with him, see. Which is strange in that we all know, any intelligent person knows that here we go again about extensions. You know. Of course we recognize that they are very fine musicians who play Dixieland. We know that. There are some that I have always admired.

But things move on, you know, we progress. So I think it's very shortsighted on his part to, you know. But anyway, I got a chance to see Kenny Clark, again, on this trip because I remember -- I've known Kenny for years when he -- I think he was playing with Edgar Hayes when I first met Kenny somewhere. I was in Cincinnati with Roy Eldridge, playing the Cotton Club, and this is where I first met Kenny.
